channel.title: Institute for Lebanon — New Documents
channel.description: Declassified U.S. State Department diplomatic cables on Lebanon's civil war and Palestinian armed presence, annotated for scholars and the public.

item.title: The Pattern Before the War: Fatah Bombs, Blackmail, and a President Who Said No
item.description: Two years before the Lebanese Civil War, the U.S. Embassy filed this cable documenting a weekend of Fatah-linked violence at Beirut International Airport. Three men including Fatah members were arrested trying to board an Air France flight with 10 kilograms of TNT. The Black September Organization threatened to blow up the airport. A 2-kilogram bomb timed to explode at 2:30 AM was found and defused in a water cooler. The Lebanese Army G-2 concluded that the bomb was planted by BSO activists acting against Arafat’s wishes — and that Arafat may have covertly helped Lebanese authorities find it. President Frangieh personally ordered his Interior Minister not to yield to the blackmail. None of this appears in the standard account of pre-war Lebanon.

item.title: The Night It Started: Emergency Cable from Beirut, 9:31 PM
item.description: At 9:31 PM on May 7, 1973, the U.S. Embassy in Beirut dispatched a Night Action Immediate cable — the highest urgency designation available — as fighting erupted across the city. The Lebanese government declared martial law at 11:30 PM. Rockets were reported landing near the airport, the Military Governorate, and the presidential palace. The most serious fighting was in the Shatila camp area. The Embassy's contacts were brief: a Presidency aide and an Army officer named Kanaan. The GOL considered the situation 'not dangerous but very serious.' Kanaan told the Embassy that Syria was playing 'the most unhelpful role' — and had no time to say more. The full picture came in a cable filed eleven hours later.

item.title: The Calm Before: Lebanon's Political House of Cards, Hours Before the Shooting
item.description: At 9:00 AM on May 7, 1973, the U.S. Embassy in Beirut filed a situation report that Washington then forwarded to Cairo. The picture it described was one of managed tension: isolated overnight incidents, Arab mediators shuttling between meetings, a Prime Minister who had just declared on television that he would not resign, and a President privately telling close sources there would be no new formal agreements — just practical tighter controls on Palestinian activity. By 10:00 PM that same evening, fighting had broken out across Beirut. By 11:30 PM, the Lebanese government had declared martial law. The calm documented in this cable lasted less than twelve hours.

item.title: Before the Civil War: The Lebanese Army Opened Fire on Palestinian Camps
item.description: At 8:08 AM on May 8, 1973, the U.S. Embassy filed this Night Action Immediate cable — the highest available urgency level. By that point, the Lebanese Army had already deployed aircraft and tanks against Palestinian refugee camps in the southeastern suburbs of Beirut: Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne. The Prime Minister had resigned at 5:00 AM. The fighting that produced this had started the previous evening — a deliberate attempt, in the Embassy's assessment, by Palestinian factions including the PDFLP, PFLP/GC, and possibly Syria's client faction Sa'iqa, to torpedo negotiations that were moving toward an accommodation. Yasser Arafat had been in those negotiations when the fighting started and was, according to U.S. sources, trying to calm his forces by morning. A ceasefire held. The Prime Minister withdrew his resignation. An agreement was reached. But the pattern documented here — armed Palestinian factions sabotaging diplomacy, Syrian manipulation of events, Lebanese state institutions stretched to breaking — repeated itself in April 1975. That time, there was no ceasefire that held.

item.title: The Verdict, Two Years Early: What the Embassy Said Lebanon Would Become
item.description: On May 12, 1973, five days after the Lebanese Army had deployed aircraft and tanks against Palestinian camps in Beirut, the U.S. Embassy filed a three-section SECRET assessment of where Lebanon stood and where it was going. The assessment covered the army's performance (good, but constrained to 6,000 combat troops), the fedayeen's strength (15,000 fighters, strategically positioned), the political situation (Sunni leaders unwilling to publicly support Frangieh on the Palestinian issue), Syria's role (decisive, minimal commitment, maximum leverage), and the three possible outcomes. The Embassy judged the best outcome — real demilitarization of the camps — unlikely. It judged the most likely outcome a face-saving compromise that would leave the underlying conditions unchanged. And it predicted, precisely, what that compromise would produce: 'seeds of another explosion.' The civil war began twenty-three months later.

item.title: The Promises They Made: The Melkart Arrangement in Real Time
item.description: On May 18, 1973, U.S. Embassy Beirut filed two classified cables 90 minutes apart documenting the conclusion of the negotiations that produced the Melkart Protocol. The first cable (1973BEIRUT05755) records the Lebanese Foreign Minister and Presidency Director-General briefing the U.S. Chargé on what had been achieved and what American diplomatic support was being requested. The second (1973BEIRUT05776) documents the specific commitments: a pullback from border areas, removal of heavy weapons from camps, no cross-border raids, Lebanese security force access to camps, and removal of non-Arab “foreign elements” — explicitly including Turks and Iranians. Both cables are marked SECRET/EXDIS. Together they confirm: the Lebanese government called these “unilateral promises,” not an agreement; Saʿiqa explicitly did not sign; the GOL’s own diplomats described fedayeen good faith as “suspect”; and Lebanese forces could enter camps only with fedayeen permission.

item.title: The Paymaster's Ledger: Arafat's Payments to Lebanese Leaders, Documented
item.description: Three weeks after the Melkart Protocol was supposed to regularize the Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon, the Lebanese Foreign Office summoned the U.S. Chargé to hand over an intelligence dossier. Secretary General Sadaqa read from Lebanese Army G-2 and Jordanian reports documenting three simultaneous developments: Iraq had offered 6,000 weapons and the USSR had delivered 2,000 Kalashnikovs at Latakia in Arafat's name; a May 21–22 fedayeen meeting decided to distribute half those weapons to Lebanese leftist groups; and Arafat had personally paid LL 250,000 to the Sunni Grand Mufti, LL 500,000 to leftist deputy Adnan Hakim, LL 100,000 to Shia leader Musa Sadr, and LL 500,000 to Kamal Jumblatt, from the Fatah treasury at Nabatiyeh. Meanwhile Syria was telling visiting Lebanese that the Lebanese government was preparing to liquidate the fedayeen — a claim the Embassy assessed as designed either to justify future Syrian action or to drive the fedayeen into preemptive attack. Sadaqa asked the U.S. to raise the matter with Moscow because the Lebanese had learned the hard way they could not trust Soviet Ambassador Azimov. The cable closes with a concrete Lebanese ask: urgent U.S. weapons for the Lebanese Army.

item.title: Trouble Ahead for Lebanon: The Embassy Warns Kissinger
item.description: On May 22, 1974 — one week after the Ma'alot attack, three days after the Israeli naval strike on Rachidiyeh camp, one day after Israeli air strikes killed three Lebanese children, and nine days before the Israeli-Syrian disengagement agreement was signed — the U.S. Embassy in Beirut filed a SECRET/LIMDIS cable addressed partly to Secretary Kissinger's travel party in Jerusalem. The message: Israeli retaliation policy is not working. It is producing civilian casualties, radicalizing Fatah moderates, strengthening Iraqi and Libyan hands, and creating a feedback loop in which every Israeli strike pushes the fedayeen toward inside-Israel operations that provoke the next Israeli strike. The cable warns that after disengagement, Iraq and Libya will work to derail it by creating Israeli-Palestinian-Lebanese trouble. It recommends a U.S. conversation with the Government of Israel about its entire policy toward Lebanon. The cable is signed GODLEY — the ambassador who would be in post when the civil war began 11 months later.

item.title: More PLO Than the PLO: Kuwait's Draft at the Arab Defense Council
item.description: On July 8, 1974, U.S. Ambassador Godley's deputy called on Presidential Adviser Boutros Dib for a readout of the July 3-4 Arab Defense Council meeting in Cairo. Dib gave him one on condition of strictest handling: SECRET/EXDIS/NOFORN, need-to-know basis only. The cable reports what Dib said: Kuwait's Foreign Minister Sabah circulated a draft resolution treating the PLO and Lebanon as equals, with LL 50 million each for defense. The Kuwaiti representative questioned Lebanese 'Arab' status — prompting PM Solh to threaten walking out. In private, the Kuwaiti FM admitted the PLO had threatened his life. The Sa'iqa representative Zuhair Mohsen was 'particularly violent,' and the Lebanese delegation believed he was personally profiting from Kuwaiti money. Syrian FM Khaddam, who had been a provocateur in 1973, played moderator in 1974. Iraq and Libya attacked Syria and Egypt for having accepted disengagement. Saudi Arabia kept its Defense Minister absent from the outset 'to save his punch for later' if the meeting went badly. The Lebanese non-Muslim ministers took pains to defend the Muslim PM from attacks by other Arabs. The final resolutions — the 'Secret Resolutions' — papered over everything.

item.title: Muddle Through Until 1976: The Embassy's October 1974 Lebanon Post-Mortem
item.description: The morning after the Solh cabinet collapsed, Ambassador G. McMurtrie Godley filed a long SECRET assessment of the 15-month Solh government and his outlook for what would follow. Solh's major accomplishment, the cable said, was to survive — by avoiding every difficult decision and bringing administrative action to a near-standstill. The cable catalogs what Solh's passivity enabled: PLO arms imports from Syria (including SA-7 missiles) with no corresponding improvement in the Lebanese Army; rising lawlessness and Iraqi-Libyan hired assassins operating in Beirut; Christian militias arming after the Turkish partition of Cyprus; the emergence of Musa as-Sadr as the political voice of Shia grievance; economic growth concentrated entirely in Beirut real estate while the south was ignored; only 11.8 percent of state revenue coming from income tax, because no one dared enforce tax laws on the well-to-do. The Embassy's prediction: Lebanon would muddle through until the 1976 elections because no force in the country saw advantage in destroying a system whose fragility was known to all. The prediction was wrong. Civil war broke out six months later, in April 1975.

item.title: Three Hours That Started a War
item.description: Three separate incidents occurred on April 13, 1975, in the Ain el-Rummaneh suburb of Beirut. The U.S. Embassy documented all three in a cable dispatched at the NIACT IMMEDIATE level — the highest available urgency designation, requiring attention regardless of the hour received — before noon the following day. The historical literature has consistently identified one of these incidents as the event that ignited Lebanon’s fifteen-year civil war. This cable contains the Embassy’s contemporaneous account of what preceded it and what followed it that same evening. Neither has been incorporated into the standard documentary record of April 13, 1975.

item.title: The Day After: Three Details the Record Does Not Carry
item.description: Filed at 3:00 PM on April 14, 1975, this situation report contains new information about the April 13 incidents that reaches the State Department record the following afternoon. Two of the four gunmen in the 9:30 AM attack that killed three Kataeb members were Libyan nationals, not Palestinians. An Iraqi-backed faction claimed 18 of the 26 people killed on the bus were its members. And the Palestinian funeral, which had been expected that morning, was deliberately postponed — in breach of standard Muslim burial practice — to allow time to organize a larger event. Each of these facts appears in this cable. None appears in the standard account.

item.title: The Second Day: What Spread Beyond Beirut
item.description: Less than 48 hours after April 13, 1975, the U.S. Embassy filed this two-section situation report as of noon on April 15. The casualty count had reached 80 to 90 throughout Lebanon. The cable documents the geographic spread of violence beyond Beirut: three Christian churches bombed in Tripoli, three non-Phalangist Christian villages near Sidon rocketed from refugee camps and then entered by armed forces. It also documents, on the basis of the Embassy’s own assessment, that the casualty balance at that point ran against the Palestinian and Muslim side — not against the Phalange.

item.title: The Ceasefire That Almost Wasn’t
item.description: Three days after April 13, 1975, the U.S. Embassy filed this situation report as of 10:00 AM on April 16. It records negotiations that had produced a nominal ceasefire. It also records two specific developments that the standard account of these events does not carry: first, that the Kataeb delivered two suspects to Lebanese government authorities as agreed, after which the PLO stated that seven — not two — were sought; and second, an unconfirmed report that PLO Chairman Arafat had favored a ceasefire for 36 hours before returning to Beirut, having been opposed during that period by his designated deputy in the city.
